newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaraguan telephone sale under review.
newsitem.headline: Nicaraguan telephone sale under review.

text.p: The Nicaraguan government was reviewing the much-delayed sale of 40 percent of its state telephone company Enitel, tentatively slated for March 31, a government official said on Monday.

"At this moment the sale of Empresa Nicaraguense de Telecomunicaciones S.A. (Enitel) is slated for March 31, 1997, however Enitel personnel have said the privatization's policies, strategies and calendar are being rigorously examined," Mario Montenegro, director of the Nicaraguan Institute of Telecomunicaciones and Mail (Telcor), told reporters.

Telcor is the government body that regulates telecommunications services in Nicaragua, including the planned privatization of Enitel. The telephone company used to carry the name Telcor but that name was changed under a privatization law.

A government commission made up of Nicaragua's finance and economy ministers, the president of Enitel, and representatives of consumers and Enitel workers was in the process of reviewing the terms of the sale to maximize the privatization's benefits to Nicaragua, Montenegro said.
Montenegro said President Arnoldo Aleman ordered the review because the market conditions for the sale of Enitel had changed since 1995 when the privatization strategy was created.
Among the changes were the inauguration of the right-wing Aleman government on Jan. 10 and the increase in the number of other countries privatizing their telephone companies, he said.

Nicaragua originally planned to announce the winning bid in for Enitel in June 1995 but the sale repeatedly has been delayed. Last year, there were two last-minute postponements, on July 27 and Oct. 3.

Nicaraguan Vice President Enrique Bolanos recently said the government postponed the last planned sale, scheduled just weeks before its Oct. 20 presidential elections, because the highest bid of $15 million made for Enitel was only "one-tenth or one-twentieth" what it wanted for the company.
He said investors were scared off by the possibility the left-wing Sandinista Front could have won the elections and this will not be a factor in the next planned privatization.

While Enitel President Pablo Ayon could not be reached for comment, in the past Enitel officials said Korea Telecom, Telefonica Internacional de Espana and the U.S. company Sprint Corp were the prime candidates to buy a stake in Enitel.
